candidates.title: Using the Aesop's Fable Paradigm to Investigate Causal Understanding of Water Displacement by New Caledonian Crows
candidates.access: PMC official-API JATS full main cached CC BY 4.0; main Methods, Results, Discussion and figure captions inspected in this run; supplemental binaries not accessed
candidates.proposed_hook: A crow can get food that is too far down a tube by dropping objects into water. But can it tell which objects and tubes actually work?

observed_findings.claim: Six wild-caught New Caledonian crows tested, with only four completing all six experiments
All birds were trained first to drop stones; not spontaneous invention of water tool use
Across 20-trial tasks, birds preferentially selected water rather than sand and sinking rather than floating objects
Four or five birds tested on later tasks; 89% solid over hollow choice, 86.8% high-water choice
Failed to prefer narrower tube on first drops; U-tube at chance (48.9%, p=0.79)

limits: Very small captive sample, four completed all six assays
Fixed task order and prior training create possible learning carryover
Failure on U-tube not proof species-wide inability or lack of all causal reasoning
Cannot claim wild stone-dropping or language-like intelligence
Supplement Data S1 and Movie S1 not inspected: do not base video claims or use footage until checked
remaining: Check PLOS CrossMark-linked corrections/expressions/retractions and context sources at source
Decide whether individual claims require Data S1; retrieve necessary supplement or omit those claims
Reconfirm reference photo taxon identification and attribution; conduct separate visual asset rights review
Create evidence and episode brief, pre-render reviewer, science script and compliant source-specific motion
Build via standard public GitHub Actions; independent exact encoded video and audio QA; SHA-bound release; archive and anonymous public bytes
Only after both-network intents/claims/month quota and readbacks, submit each separate destination

candidates.title: Behavioral evidence for two-stage sleep in spiders
candidates.access: PMC official-API JATS full main cached CC BY 4.0; introduction, primary Methods/Results and Discussion inspected; four supplemental binaries not accessed
candidates.proposed_hook: How do you tell a sleeping spider from one that is merely sitting still? Interrupt its night and see what happens next.

observed_findings.claim: Juvenile/captive Portia studied in distinct experiments; 40 for circadian locomotion, 10 sleep architecture, 30 arousal
observed_findings.location: Materials and Methods > Circadian activity tracking, Sleep architecture, Arousal threshold

observed_findings.claim: Sleep architecture: 10 spiders, 109 REM-like bouts, but sleep window potentially includes quiet wakefulness
observed_findings.location: Results > Sleep Architecture and Discussion limitations

observed_findings.claim: At standardized acoustic stimulus, response longer in REM-like than waking state, 4.27 versus 1.69 seconds among responding spiders; four of ten REM-like spiders did not respond within ten-second test
After fly-induced interrupted night, n=13 usable rebound recordings; total REM-like time 9.4 to 16.9 min and number of REM-like bouts increased
observed_findings.location: Results > Sleep Disruption; Methods > Sleep homeostasis

observed_findings.claim: Undisturbed control n=5 did not show same increase in sleep window

limits: Strong behavioral evidence for sleep and REM-like state, not evidence of dreaming or mammalian-equivalent REM brain activity
No electrophysiological measurement; some quiet wakefulness possible
Fly exposure was sleep disruption not proven complete deprivation; disrupted night not filmed continuously
Multiple distinct modest-sized experimental samples, some exclusions; not a single N=92 comparison
Do not reuse research supplement imagery/audio without separate licensing, and no claim of watching it
